source: Webb, Little, Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem: investigating insight across task types
finding: Solvers rated aha on a continuous scale after classic insight problems, compound remote associates (CRA) and non-insight problems. The task label did not fix how much insight was reported. Aha tracked accuracy for insight problems and CRAs, and barely for non-insight problems in Exp 1.
numbers: Exp 1 (193 recruited, 9 dropped; Melbourne undergrads): correlation of aha with accuracy r=0.50 insight problems, r=0.41 CRAs, r=0.02 non-insight (BF10<1). Problem type effect on accuracy BF10>150, eta-sq 0.22; CRA accuracy 14 points below insight problems. Exp 1a (N=82): r=0.40, 0.40, 0.24 (non-insight p=0.04). Exp 2 (N=129): r=0.495, 0.39, 0.19.
quote: Insight problems are not in the problem
limits: Task effects on accuracy were large and partly driven by low CRA accuracy in ESL students. Aha was rated after solving, so it may be a reaction to success rather than a marker of the process. Authors say they cannot separate a feeling of insight from an insight process.
agent_relevance: Do not use the task type as the label for insight in an S6 test set. Label by what the run did (a representation shift) and test with problems that have a checkable answer.

source: Webb, Little, Cropper (2016) multilevel logistic model, Exps 1, 1a, 2 pooled
finding: In a pooled model for native English speakers, rated aha, surprise and impasse all predicted whether a solution was correct, but in different directions. Aha raised accuracy, impasse lowered it, surprise lowered it.
numbers: Best model by BIC (BIC 5627.8 vs 5839.0 for the simplest) had subject-level random effects for problem type. Feeling of impasse decreased accuracy, surprise decreased accuracy, aha increased accuracy.
limits: Correlational. Ratings made after the answer. Cannot say whether the feeling caused the correct answer.
agent_relevance: A reported feeling of being stuck (impasse) is a cue of failure, not of insight. An S6 detector should not treat stuck language as a sign that a breakthrough is near.

source: Webb, Little, Cropper (2016) the discrepancy with Metcalfe (1986)
finding: Metcalfe found that feeling suddenly close (high warmth) often marked a wrong answer. Salvi et al. found that self-labelled insight answers are right more often. Webb et al. argue the two disagree because of the measure: warmth ratings taken during the attempt versus a binary label taken after the answer.
numbers: Salvi et al. (2016) found insight was reported in only 51.9% of correct trials (as quoted by Webb). Webb et al. note 70% of continuous ratings were not at the scale ends and 35% were in the inner quartile range, so a binary split at 50 would discard real information.
limits: Reasoning in the discussion, not a direct test of the two measures.
agent_relevance: When we log a confidence or closeness signal in S6, record when it was taken (before or after the answer) and as a graded value, not only yes or no.

source: Laukkonen and Tangen (2018) How to detect insight moments in problem solving experiments
finding: Two common insight measures barely agree. The warmth measure (sudden jump from cold to solved) and the self-report of an aha moment pick out different problems. Self-report is the better measure of what researchers mean by insight.
numbers: N=80 undergraduates, 20 verbal insight problems, 1 min each, warmth rated every 10 s. Of 631 correct solutions, 180 had 2 or more warmth ratings. Per participant the counts correlated r=0.61 (n=51) but per problem r=0.08 (n=182, p=0.235). If warmth said sudden, 75.6% were self-reported insight. If warmth said gradual, 50.8% were still self-reported insight.
quote: Out of a possible 631 correctly solved insight problems, participants provided two or more warmth ratings in 180 cases.
limits: Verbal problems only, one lab, 180 usable cases. Authors state there is no ground truth, so the choice rests on argument. Warmth ratings may be reactive.
agent_relevance: Gradual progress ratings do not rule out a sudden restructuring. Measure the restructuring itself in our traces (did the problem representation change) and do not infer it from smooth confidence.

source: Laukkonen and Tangen (2018) claim that warmth has data loss and reactive cost
finding: Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) needed at least three warmth ratings per problem. Many problems are solved in under 30 s, so data are lost. The authors use a two-rating differential warmth score instead.
numbers: In Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987), only 39 of 73 subjects gave usable data. Metcalfe and Wiebe used ratings every 10 s, Metcalfe (1986) every 10 s and 15 s in experiment two.
limits: Statement about the original study as quoted in a later paper, not the original text.
agent_relevance: Any step-by-step progress probe has a coverage cost. Short runs give no curve.

source: Danek and Wiley (2017) What about false insights? Deconstructing the Aha experience
finding: People report strong aha moments for wrong answers too. Correct solutions got higher aha ratings, but a large share of wrong ones did as well.
numbers: N=70, 35 magic-trick videos, 1778 solution attempts; 36.8% correct (654), 63.2% wrong (1124). Aha mean 66.50 (SD 18.42) correct versus 52.34 (SD 18.78) wrong, t(69)=10.21. 37% of wrong solutions (417 of 1124) were rated above the average for correct ones. Correct solutions were faster: 35.81 s versus 42.46 s, t(1776)=6.26.
limits: Magic tricks, not classic insight problems. Participants chose when to give a solution, and 603 trials timed out.
agent_relevance: A false aha is a real event. An LLM line like 'I see it now' is not evidence the solution is right, and a verification step is still needed.

source: Danek and Wiley (2017) dimensions of aha
finding: Aha has several parts. Pleasure, suddenness and certainty were the unique predictors of the overall aha rating for both correct and wrong solutions. Correct solutions added relief, wrong ones added surprise.
numbers: Pearson correlations with the global aha rating, N=1778 trials: pleasure 0.66, certainty 0.58, suddenness 0.49, relief 0.49, drive 0.28, surprise 0.07. Webb et al. had found surprise correlating 0.29 to 0.48 with aha.
limits: Task differs from Webb et al. (magic tricks versus mixed problems), so the surprise difference may be task-driven. Single lab.
agent_relevance: If a test set asks for graded self-report, use pleasure, suddenness and certainty items, and do not ask for surprise alone.

source: Danek and Wiley (2017) timing cue for false insight
finding: Fast wrong answers got high aha scores. Slow wrong answers got low scores. Solvers seem to use speed as a cue for how insightful the answer was.
numbers: Mixed model: aha rose with faster solution time (t=4.03, p<0.01); correctness main effect t=-3.36; interaction t=1.58, p<0.12 (not significant).
limits: Interaction not significant, so the claim about different slopes for wrong answers is suggestive only.
agent_relevance: Response latency in tokens or steps may leak into any self-rated confidence. Control for length when comparing rated confidence across items.

source: Hedne, Norman, Metcalfe (2016) Intuitive feelings of warmth and confidence in insight and noninsight problem solving of magic tricks
finding: Solutions that people called insight were more accurate and more confident, but warmth did not differ between insight and non-insight solutions. This is a failure to find the classic sudden-warmth signature.
numbers: 32 magic-trick videos of 15 s, 971 included trials; 29% called insight. Accuracy 0.57 (insight) vs 0.37 (non-insight), d=0.51. Confidence 78.32 vs 68.95, d=0.50. Differential warmth 12.93 vs 11.65, d=0.07, p=0.47. Solution time 38.23 s vs 40.56 s, p=0.089.
limits: Eight participants who reported no aha were dropped, and trials with several answers were dropped. Confidence tracked accuracy more tightly in non-insight trials, and for insight trials wrong answers were more often repeated later (0.72 vs 0.61, d=0.23).
agent_relevance: Insight-labelled answers are both more accurate and more stubborn. A wrong answer reached with a feeling of insight is harder to dislodge, so S6 verification must be independent of the confidence.

source: Kizilirmak, Serger, Kehl, Richardson-Klavehn (2018) Feelings-of-warmth increase more abruptly for verbal riddles solved with aha
finding: With compound remote associates, warmth rose more steeply in the last two ratings when the solution came with aha. This partly supports the sudden-jump account, and contradicts Hedne et al. on a different task.
numbers: 96 German CRAT items per person, 30 s per round. Aha more often reported for self-generated solutions than for solutions shown after failure: P(aha) 0.76 (SD 0.27) vs 0.57 (SD 0.29), F(1,35)=6.26, p=0.017. Last-two-rating warmth rise 2.59 (SD 0.97) with aha vs 1.43 (SD 1.07) without, t(26)=4.27, p<0.001. For items solved in four rounds the curves overlapped.
limits: Rise is steeper but not a pure jump; warmth was still gradual before the last steps, which the authors read as support for a continuous model. Exposure of the solution lifted aha less, so aha depends on who produced the answer.
agent_relevance: Producing an answer yourself and being shown it feel different. If an agent is handed a hint or answer by a tool, do not count that as an insight event.

source: Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving
finding: The founding warmth study. Insight problems showed a sudden cold-to-solved pattern. Multi-step and algebra problems showed gradual warmth growth.
numbers: As described in Laukkonen and Tangen (2018): warmth every 10 s; only 39 of 73 subjects gave usable data. Not opened here.
limits: Not read this session. Later work (Hedne 2016, Laukkonen and Tangen 2018) failed to reproduce a clean warmth split on other tasks.
agent_relevance: The origin of the warmth probe. Treat the sudden/gradual split as task-dependent.

source: Salvi, Bricolo, Kounios, Bowden, Beeman (2016) Insight solutions are correct more often than analytic solutions
finding: Four experiments with linguistic, visual and mixed puzzles. Answers the solver labelled as insight were more often correct than answers labelled analytic.
numbers: As reported in press summaries and Webb et al.: linguistic puzzles 94% correct for insight vs 78% analytic; visual 78% vs 42%; for visual puzzles 72% of answers in the last 5 s were wrong. Only 51.9% of correct trials were labelled insight (Webb et al.).
limits: Full text not read (the PMC fetch failed). Numbers from secondary sources, so check before reuse. Time pressure means analytic answers include rushed guesses.
agent_relevance: Supports a mild rule: an answer reached with a sudden shift is a slightly better bet than a rushed guess. But see Danek and Wiley for false insights.

source: Webb, Laukkonen, Cropper, Little (2018) Commentary: Moment of (perceived) truth: exploring accuracy of aha experiences
finding: A reply to Danek and Salvi (2018). The aha feeling can be manipulated independently of accuracy, and there are erroneous insights and a disposition to feel insight, so aha is not proof that the answer is right.
numbers: Cites Topolinski and Reber (2010): shorter delay between question and shown answer made answers seem truer. Laukkonen et al. (2020): solving an anagram of a key word with aha made the following general-knowledge claim (e.g. kangaroos keep growing until they die) seem more true.
limits: Commentary, argument backed by cited studies. Numbers are not given in the text.
agent_relevance: An aha-like event can leak into the next judgement. After an apparent breakthrough, check the next claim as strictly as the last one.

source: Ash and Wiley (2006) The nature of restructuring in insight: an individual-differences approach
finding: Working memory span predicted success on problems with a large faulty search space and on the restructuring phase mixed in, but not on problems built to isolate restructuring. This points to automatic spread of activation for restructuring, not controlled search.
numbers: Regression of correct count on WM measures R-squared about .08, F(2,112) (as printed in text). Matched problem sets: one with large initial search space, one constrained. 3 participants dropped for incomplete data.
limits: Small effects. Individual-difference correlations are indirect evidence. Only a few problem types.
agent_relevance: Restructuring may not be something more effort or a bigger memory buys. Supports using a prompt trigger (switch the frame) instead of just longer thinking.

source: Ash, Cushen, Wiley (2009) Obstacles in investigating the role of restructuring in insightful problem solving
finding: Names three assumptions behind restructuring theories (representational difficulty, representational change, discontinuity of solution) and argues each needs direct testing before restructuring is treated as different from ordinary search. Lists theoretical and methodological obstacles and recommendations.
numbers: No numbers; the full PDF (viewcontent.cgi, 805 KB) returned 403, so only the abstract page was read.
limits: Abstract only. Do not quote detail from the body.
agent_relevance: Defines what an S6 test must show: that the problem is hard because of the initial representation, that the representation changed, and that solving was not a smooth search.

source: Weisberg (2015) Toward an integrated theory of insight in problem solving
finding: Business-as-usual view: insight is explained by the same conscious processes as other problem solving, with restructuring as the extra feature, and impasse is not required.
numbers: Described in secondary summaries (2021 Consciousness and Cognition paper): impasse was not a prerequisite for insight. No numbers.
limits: Not opened; relied on a search snippet.
agent_relevance: Supports treating an impasse trigger as optional. Some good solutions come with no stuck phase.

source: Danek et al. (2014) / Klein and Jarosz (2011) / Fleck and Weisberg (2013) as cited by Laukkonen and Tangen (2018)
finding: Even classic insight problems are often solved without insight, by a variety of strategies. Danek et al. add that insight problems per se do not exist, only solutions with insight.
numbers: No new numbers in the quoting paper; Bowden and Jung-Beeman (2007) is said to make the same point.
quote: even so-called insight problems are often solved without insight
limits: Second-hand statement of those studies; the originals were not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a puzzle labelled insight needs insight. Score the process on every item.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo benchmark: Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight
finding: 38 LLMs scored far below humans on Japanese riddles that need a representation shift. Reasoning models roughly doubled the odds of success but stayed under 20%.
numbers: 201 riddles; 120-item human subset. Humans about 52.9% (pilot N=126, mean 10.58 of 20, SD 7.11, bimodal with peaks at 0 and 20). Non-reasoning models (n=16) 7.60%, reasoning (n=19) 17.59%. Pooled odds ratio 2.29 (95% CI 1.99 to 2.64). Reasoning minus non-reasoning 9.8 points, d=0.946. Model size did not predict accuracy (r=-0.017); release date did (Spearman 0.402, p=0.0123).
limits: Japanese wordplay, so partly a language test. Zero-shot, single answer, no metacognitive prompting. Human sample is a survey, not a lab. Candidate-tracking in logs is informal.
agent_relevance: A direct template for an S6 test set: short items, checkable single answers, fresh items can be generated, a bimodal human baseline. Reasoning scaffolds help, but the gap to humans stays large.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo: verification failure and false aha in thought logs
finding: Models often wrote the right answer and then did not pick it (verification failure). They also wrote aha-style exclamations before wrong answers. Models said they were stuck, backtracked, and used feeling words as signs of rightness or wrongness.
numbers: Claude-opus-4 wrote 'Oh! I just...' more than 100 times, with correct answers rare after such lines. Gemini-2.5-flash-preview said it was stuck 9 times and 'I am back to...' 29 times. Claude-opus-4 said stuck 3 times, Grok-4 2 times. Overall accuracy: Grok-4 37.6%, DeepSeek-R1-0528 about 22.9%, Claude-opus-4 about 30.3%, Gemini-2.5-flash-preview 10.9% (column assignment as printed).
limits: Qualitative log reading, the authors say it is hypothesis-generating. Chain of thought may not show the real computation. No blind rating of aha statements.
agent_relevance: Two failures our schema can target: do not trust an 'aha' phrase, and when a candidate matches the checkable form of the answer, stop and commit. A separate commit check (fit to the riddle's rule) is cheap.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo: language of thought and accuracy
finding: Thinking in Japanese did not help on Japanese riddles. Some models thought in English even when asked in Japanese.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-flash-preview: about 15 lines per question in English versus about 209 in Japanese, with 0 of 12 Japanese-thought answers correct. Grok-4: English 40/82 (48.8%) vs Japanese 33/112 (29.5%) correct, p=0.0071. Claude-opus-4: Japanese 16/44 (36.7%) vs English 45/157 (28.7%), no significant difference (not significant).
limits: Choice of language was not randomised, so harder items may drive it. Small cell counts.
agent_relevance: Do not force a language for the scaffold. Tell the model to restate the item in the form that exposes the wordplay.

source: Alavi Naeini et al. (2023) LLMs are fixated by red herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset
finding: On quiz-show puzzles with built-in red herrings (a proxy for remote associates tests), GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 did far worse than humans. Removing red herrings raised the scores sharply, which supports a fixation account.
numbers: Human connection accuracy about 80%. GPT-4 grouping, 0-shot: 6 solved walls, 239 correct groups; best few-shot 7 walls (5-shot), 272 groups (3-shot). GPT-3.5 0-shot: 0 walls, 114 groups. Connection-naming F1 41 to 45 for GPT-4 10-shot. Red herrings reduced (OCW-WordNet): GPT-3.5 0-shot 337 solved walls and 1522 groups versus 0 and 114 on the original.
limits: No chain-of-thought or tree search was tried. OCW-WordNet also changes the task type (hierarchy and synonyms), so it is not a clean red-herring ablation. Models are 2023 vintage.
agent_relevance: Fixation by plausible distractors is measurable in LLMs. Test sets for S6 should include matched item pairs with and without a strong decoy.

source: Speed (2023) Assessing the nature of large language models: a caution against anthropocentrism
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 did surprisingly badly on a Remote Associates Test, but better on insight problems. Item difficulty for the model did not track item difficulty for people.
numbers: RAT triplets: human pass rate 9% to 85% per item; GPT-3.5 ranged 0% to 100% across 4 runs; correlation of human and GPT-3.5 item rates r=0.39. Insight problems (5 items): human 44% to 61% per item; GPT-3.5 1.5 to 3.5 of 5; GPT-4 4.5 of 5 (one run); human versus GPT-3.5 item correlation r=-0.63 on 4 observations. Many correct RAT answers came with wrong explanations (10 of 22 triplets in one run).
limits: Tiny sample, 2023 models, unaligned study design, authors warn the negative correlation rests on four observations. Not peer reviewed as far as shown.
agent_relevance: Do not assume items hard for people are hard for the model. Calibrate the S6 test set on model pass rates, and score the stated reason as well as the answer.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: lateral thinking puzzles for large language models
finding: A 1,100-puzzle multiple-choice benchmark of lateral thinking, with semantic and context rewrites to check for memorisation. ChatGPT scored about halfway between chance and humans.
numbers: Sentence puzzles and word puzzles. ChatGPT 53% and 63%; random 25%; human 92% (3 experts on 102 questions). Group accuracy (original plus both rewrites all correct) is lower than item accuracy. Annotators rated 99% of original items valid, 100% of semantic and 97% of context rewrites consistent.
limits: Multiple choice reduces generation, which is the hard part of insight. Common-sense-augmented models sometimes did worse. Later work (cited in NazoNazo) reports GPT-4 with metacognitive prompting above 98%, so this set is now close to saturation.
agent_relevance: Group-based scoring over rewrites is a good guard: a real shift should survive rewording. Use it in our S6 set.

source: d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro (2026) The illusion of insight in reasoning models
finding: Mid-trace 'wait, let's re-evaluate' shifts are rare and usually go with lower accuracy. They are signs of unstable inference, not of intrinsic insight. But forcing a reconsideration when the model is uncertain does raise accuracy.
numbers: Over 1M reasoning traces, GRPO runs of Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B and Llama 3.1-8B on crosswords, MATH-500 and Rush Hour. Shifts in 6.31% of traces overall (about 7.6% for the core models). Accuracy 2.57% with a shift versus 16.44% without. Entropy-gated forced reconsideration (top 20% entropy) gave +8.41 points on MATH-500, smaller gains on crosswords and Rush Hour. Training did not make shifts more frequent. Example checkpoint gains: Qwen2.5-1.5B math 31.00 to 35.00.
limits: Small open models. The shift detector is a pipeline with an LLM judge and a rubric. Gains come from an external trigger, not spontaneous insight.
agent_relevance: Strongest support for our design: do not wait for a spontaneous aha. Gate a forced re-represent step on a code-side uncertainty signal.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Understanding aha moments: from external observations to internal mechanisms
finding: Studies aha moments in reasoning models by language pattern, uncertainty and latent space. Claims aha-trained models use more human-like self-reflection, adjust uncertainty to difficulty and avoid 'reasoning collapse'.
numbers: Abstract-level claims read; the full result tables were not extracted. Introduces RASM, a log-probability metric for the split between human-like tone and pure reasoning.
limits: Conflicts with d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro (2026), who report shifts mostly hurt accuracy. Differences in definition: Yang et al. count tone and uncertainty, not a gain on previously failed problems.
agent_relevance: Surface markers of aha are cheap to see and weak as evidence. Use a performance-based definition (failed before, solved after the shift).

source: Latif et al. (2024) RAT result as cited in the NazoNazo paper
finding: Latif et al. (2024) is cited as showing that state-of-the-art models may already beat humans on the RAT and classic insight tasks. This contrasts with Speed (2023) and with NazoNazo.
numbers: No numbers given in the citing paper. The cited Latif 2024 paper was not opened here.
limits: Second-hand claim. Differences across studies could come from model version, prompt and scoring.
agent_relevance: Treat RAT as near saturated for frontier models and do not rely on it for S6 testing.

source: Kizilirmak et al. (2018) task mix: share of insight solutions across tasks
finding: The discussion compares the share of solutions reported with aha across studies: CRAT items, Mooney images and magic tricks give different rates. Aha rates depend on task and on whether the solver generated the answer.
numbers: Mooney-image figure of 29% of solved generated solutions quoted; Hedne et al. magic tricks 29% called insight; P(aha) for generated CRAT solutions 0.76. Exact source of the 29% Mooney figure is not stated in the lines read.
limits: Cross-study comparison with different instructions for what counts as aha (Cushen and Wiley used only surprise and suddenness).
agent_relevance: Because the definition of aha varies by lab, any claim about insight frequency needs the exact instruction wording copied into our test.

source: Wikipedia and field record: laboratory insight tasks may not reflect real insight; naturalistic work shows gradual insight
finding: Background from the SUBFIELDS record: some argue lab tasks do not reflect real insight, and field accounts describe insight as gradual. The Webb commentary also notes that Klein and Jarosz (2011) found insight in firefighting and mathematics.
numbers: Not opened; one line in the SUBFIELDS table and one line of the commentary (mathematics and firefighting).
limits: Weak: no numbers, secondary.
agent_relevance: Keep a naturalistic test (extended, many-step tasks) next to puzzle sets, because puzzles overstate suddenness.
